title: Parachute Drop: Fall Slowly, Land Softly
description: A napkin canopy, four strings and a brave paper-clip passenger. Build a parachute, label its parts, and find out why a big canopy falls so gently.

body.heading: Falling, but politely
paragraphs: Drop a paper clip and it plummets. Drop the same clip under a parachute and it floats down like a dandelion seed. Nothing about gravity changed — the parachute simply gives the falling air something big to push against. Build one and watch falling slow down.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The canopy — the napkin or square of light fabric or plastic that catches the air. The lines — four strings, all the same length, that share the passenger's weight evenly. The passenger — a paper clip, washer or tiny toy that the parachute must protect. The vent — the small hole at the canopy's top that lets a little air escape so the parachute doesn't wobble and spill.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: A paper napkin or a square cut from a thin plastic bag, four pieces of string the same length, tape, a paper clip or small washer as the passenger, safety scissors, and a ruler for measuring the strings evenly.

paragraphs: Step 1 — Make the canopy. Lay the napkin flat. Tape one string to each corner, pressing the tape down firmly — corners are where parachutes fail.
Step 2 — Gather the lines. Hold the four free ends together, check they are exactly the same length (uneven lines make tippy parachutes), and tie or tape them to the passenger.
Step 3 — Pack it loosely. Hold the passenger in one hand and let the canopy drape over it — no careful folding needed; parachutes like to be scruffy.

Step 4 — Drop! A grown-up approves the spot — the top of the stairs or a chair they hold steady. Hold the parachute high by the canopy's middle, let the passenger dangle, and release. Time the fall with a slow count. Then drop the passenger alone and count again.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: Falling things are pulled by gravity but pushed back by the air they shove aside — that push is air resistance, or drag. A wide canopy shoves aside a LOT of air, so the push-back nearly matches gravity's pull, and the fall slows to a gentle drift. It is why real parachutes are enormous: a person needs a canopy the size of a room to catch enough air. The little vent hole matters too — it lets trapped air leak out steadily so the canopy floats straight instead of rocking and spilling its air.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Why must all four strings be exactly the same length?
2. Predict: a canopy twice as big — does the passenger fall faster, slower, or the same? How could you test fairly?

takeaway: A parachute falls slowly because its wide canopy catches so much air that air resistance nearly balances gravity's pull.
materials: Paper napkin or square of thin plastic bag (canopy)
supervision: A grown-up supervises every drop and chooses the drop spot; children never climb to drop from height themselves.
safetyNotes: Drops happen from a spot a grown-up approves and controls — the top of stairs with a grown-up present, or a chair a grown-up holds. Never drop from windows, balconies a child can climb to, or furniture a child stands on alone.
Keep the drop zone clear: nobody stands underneath a falling passenger, even a paper clip.
Plastic-bag canopies: use only with a grown-up present, and store bags away afterwards — plastic bags are never toys for younger children and never go near faces.
screenFreeExtension: Canopy trials: make a second parachute with a bigger napkin and race the two, counting the fall out loud — record which canopy wins three drops in a row.
